milestones.title: Alexander the Great founds Alexandria
milestones.detail: Alexander had a Greek city laid out on a grid by the architect Dinocrates, beside the Egyptian village of Rhakotis and behind the island of Pharos. He left a few months later and never returned.

milestones.title: Ptolemy I makes Alexandria his capital
milestones.detail: Ptolemy declared himself king in 305 BCE and moved the capital from Memphis. Within a century Alexandria was the largest city in the world.

milestones.title: Pharos lighthouse built
milestones.detail: The lighthouse on Pharos island, commissioned by Ptolemy I and finished under Ptolemy II, took twelve years to build and stood over 100 m tall.

milestones.title: Caesar's siege of Alexandria
milestones.detail: Julius Caesar was besieged in the city in 47 BCE, and the royal Library was damaged in the fighting. Octavian (Augustus) later placed the city under a Roman prefect.

milestones.title: Caracalla's massacre
milestones.detail: The emperor Caracalla, visiting in 215, ordered his troops to kill the city's young men and a general massacre followed. The city lost trade and population through the 3rd century.

milestones.title: Diocletian takes the city after a long siege
milestones.detail: Diocletian besieged and captured Alexandria in 297-298 to suppress a usurper. The column known as Pompey's Pillar was raised in his honour.

milestones.title: Tsunami strikes the city
milestones.detail: The tsunami that followed the Crete earthquake of 21 July 365 devastated Alexandria and the Nile Delta, killing thousands. The day was still commemorated in the city two centuries later.

milestones.title: Arab conquest; the capital moves to Fustat
milestones.detail: Amr ibn al-As took Alexandria after a fourteen-month siege. Egypt's capital moved to the new city of Fustat, and Alexandria shrank to a provincial port.

milestones.title: Earthquake ruins the Pharos
milestones.detail: Earthquakes in 956 and above all 1303 wrecked the lighthouse; Ibn Battuta found it partly in ruins in 1326 and impossible to enter in 1349.

milestones.title: Cypriot crusaders sack the city
milestones.detail: A crusade led by Peter I of Cyprus took Alexandria in October 1365 and held it for three days. About 20,000 civilians are reported killed and 5,000 enslaved.
milestones.source: Mikaberidze (2011), Conflict and Conquest in the Islamic World, vol. 1, p. 72, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandrian_Crusade

milestones.title: Citadel of Qaitbay built
milestones.detail: The Mamluk sultan Qaitbay built a fort on the site of the ruined lighthouse, reusing its last stones.

milestones.title: French capture a much-reduced town
milestones.detail: Napoleon's troops stormed Alexandria on 2 July 1798. Around 1800 the town had only about 8,000 inhabitants.
milestones.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandria#Islamic_era ; Reimer (1988), 'Colonial Bridgehead: Social and Spatial Change in Alexandria, 1850-1882', International Journal of Middle East Studies 20(4), pp. 531-553, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Alexandria

milestones.title: Mahmudiyya Canal opens
milestones.detail: The canal ordered by Muhammad Ali in 1817 brought Nile water and shipping to Alexandria. Rebuilding began around 1810, and by 1850 the city had regained something of its former standing.

milestones.title: Cairo-Alexandria railway begins operating
milestones.detail: The railway to Cairo opened in 1856, followed by a new port in 1865-1869 during the cotton boom.

milestones.title: British bombardment
milestones.detail: After anti-European riots, a British fleet bombarded Alexandria on 11 July 1882 at the start of the occupation of Egypt.
milestones.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombardment_of_Alexandria ; Reimer (1988), 'Colonial Bridgehead: Social and Spatial Change in Alexandria, 1850-1882', International Journal of Middle East Studies 20(4), pp. 531-553, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Alexandria

milestones.title: Departure of the foreign communities
milestones.detail: Europeans began leaving after the 1956 Suez Crisis, and the nationalisations that peaked in 1961 drove out nearly all the rest.

milestones.title: Bibliotheca Alexandrina inaugurated
milestones.detail: A new library and cultural centre, built on the seafront near the harbour to a design by Snohetta, opened in October 2002.

landmarks.name: Pharos (Lighthouse of Alexandria)
landmarks.source: McKenzie (2011), The Architecture of Alexandria and Egypt: 300 BC - AD 700, p. 42, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lighthouse_of_Alexandria (Arab descriptions give 103 to 118 m; built in the reign of Ptolemy II, 280-247 BC)
landmarks.note: Height is the lower end of the 103-118 m range from medieval Arab descriptions. The construction year is approximate. The tower was ruined by the 1303 earthquake; its last remains were built into the Citadel of Qaitbay in about 1480.

landmarks.name: Pompey's Pillar
landmarks.source: Delbrück (2007), pp. 100-101, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pompey%27s_Pillar (26.85 m including base and capital; built 298-303)
landmarks.note: Height as it stands; it originally carried a statue of Diocletian about 7 m tall.

landmarks.name: Abu al-Abbas al-Mursi Mosque
landmarks.note: Height is that of the minaret. Earlier mosques stood on the site from 1307.

landmarks.name: Bibliotheca Alexandrina
landmarks.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bibliotheca_Alexandrina (main reading room beneath a 32-metre-high roof; inaugurated 2002)

notes: Start date: the founding by Alexander is securely documented but sources give either 332 BCE (Britannica 1911) or April 331 BCE (the date used here). An Egyptian village, Rhakotis, already stood on the shore and became the Egyptian quarter; radiocarbon evidence also shows activity on the site in the Old Kingdom and around 1000-800 BCE, but not a continuous town. Population: ancient figures are scholarly estimates that disagree widely. Modelski's series is used to 400 CE and Chandler's afterwards; where both give a figure for the same date the alternative is in the note. Modelski's 1,000,000 for 100 BCE is left out as an outlier (he gives 400,000 a century later), and so are the digitised Chandler values of 160,000 for 881 and 175,000 for 900, which contradict both Modelski (100,000) and the city's known contraction after the capital moved to Fustat and look like transcription errors. There is no figure between 860 and 1150 or between 1500 and 1693. The long decline to about 8,000 people in 1800 and the very rapid 19th-century recovery are recorded as the sources give them; Chandler's 134,000 for 1848 is omitted in favour of Reimer's series. Census figures from 1897 are for the city's qisms. Landmarks: only six structures had a sourced height. The Pharos height is an estimate from medieval descriptions and the Citadel and Bibliotheca heights come from Wikipedia without a strong citation. No height could be sourced for the Serapeum, the Caesareum and Cleopatra's Needles (removed 1877-1880), the Roman theatre at Kom el-Dikka, Montaza Palace, Ras el-Tin Palace, St Mark's Cathedral, Stanley Bridge or Borg El Arab Stadium, so they are omitted.
